pinboard.title: Kids can bypass some age checks with a drawn-on mustache
pinboard.description:
It’s been months since the UK government began requiring stronger age checks under the Online Safety Act, and recent research suggests those measures are falling short of keeping kids away from harmful content. In some cases, even drawing on a mustache has been reported as enough to fool age detection software.

Like keeping booze away from teenagers or nudie mags out of the hands of young lads, slapping a big “restricted, 18+” label on parts of the internet hasn't stopped kids testing the limits. Those limits, according to UK online safety group Internet Matters, are easy to sidestep.

The group surveyed over 1,000 UK children and their parents, and while it did report some positive effects from changes made under the OSA, many children saw age verification as an easy-to-bypass hurdle rather than something that kept them genuinely safe.

A full 46 percent of children even said that age checks were easy to bypass, while just 17 percent said that they were difficult to fool. The methods kids use to fool age gates vary, but most are pretty simple: There's the classic use of a video game character to fool video selfie systems, while in other instances, children reported just entering a fake birthday or using someone else's ID card when that was required. 

The report even cites cases of children drawing a mustache on their faces to fool age detection filters. Seriously.

pinboard.title: AI Doesn't Fix Accessible Systems. It Depends on Them. — Anna E. Cook
pinboard.description:
For the last few years, our industry has been told a story: AI will personalize its way out of accessibility, deterministic design is dead, diagnosis can replace systems thinking, and structural work no longer needs to be done.

None of it is true. AI cannot repair a broken structure. Instead, AI inherits it and reproduces it at scale.

The logic actually runs the other way:

- Accessible systems are structured.
- Structured systems are parseable.
- Parseable systems are AI-interpretable.

Accessibility advocates have been designing for this variability for decades. We didn’t need AI to create interfaces that were dynamic. We were already working in that reality. What AI actually did was make variability more visible to people who hadn’t been looking.

our industry keeps telling us to identify the condition, then design. This framing is backwards. It’s part of why so many accessibility overlays don’t work. People experience friction first. Labels come later, if they even come at all. 

This is adaptive design. It ensures people with and without a diagnosis can better use what we build. Adaptive design starts with variability, anticipating multiple valid paths without requiring anyone to prove they need one. Instead of predicting identity, it supports agency.

This is the one that gets me most: the myth that AI can repair broken structure.

AI doesn’t fix that. It learns from it. It generates based on what it was trained on. It reproduces the errors, not as static bugs we can catch and file, but as probabilistic failures distributed unpredictably across outputs.

AI does not repair broken systems. It multiplies them.

LLMs and Gen AI have been trained on a highly inaccessible and deeply flawed dataset — publicly available “free” data on the good ol’ World Wide Web.  

Models can sometimes generate helpful alt text suggestions or accessible code when explicitly prompted to do so, but accessibility shouldn’t depend on a well-crafted prompt. 

As of today, AI amplifies the structure it’s given. Make the structure better, and we get more resilient output. Leave the structure broken, and we’ve just made the problems harder to find.

Not every product needs AI. But every product needs accessible, well-designed systems.

Accessible infrastructure makes systems structured, resilient, and trustworthy. It protects people whether they choose to use AI or not. It redistributes power not through personalization, but by strengthening the baseline — by building systems that meet more people, in more conditions, more reliably.

If our system is accessible, it is structured. If it is structured, it is parseable. If it is parseable, AI can interpret it and create from it.
